notes.front: What is attitude instrument flying?
notes.back: Controlling an aircraft’s spatial position by using instruments rather than outside visual references.
notes.explanation: In visual flight the pilot uses the natural horizon; in instrument flight the flight instruments give essentially the same information.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Introduction”, PDF p. 134
notes.evidence: Attitude instrument flying is defined as the control of an aircraft’s spatial position by using instruments rather than outside visual references.
notes.example: Like driving in thick fog by the dashboard and a lane-keeping display instead of looking out of the windscreen.

notes.front: What is the control and performance method?
notes.back: Flying by setting attitude and power on the control instruments, then checking the performance instruments and adjusting.
notes.explanation: Performance follows from attitude plus power, so the pilot sets those and uses the results to correct them.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Attitude Instrument Flying Using the Control and Performance Method”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: Aircraft performance is achieved by controlling the aircraft
notes.example: Like cooking by setting the oven dial and timer first, then checking the cake and adjusting next time.

notes.front: What is the primary and supporting method?
notes.back: A teaching method that groups instruments by control function (pitch, bank, power, trim) and names primary and supporting instruments for each.
notes.explanation: For each control function, the primary instrument gives the most pertinent information for the manoeuvre; the others support it.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Attitude Instrument Flying Using the Primary and Supporting Method”, PDF p. 137
notes.evidence: classifies the instruments as they relate to control function,
notes.example: Like a sports team where one player leads each play while the others back them up, and the lead changes with the play.

notes.front: What is the instrument cross-check?
notes.back: The continuous and logical observation of the instruments for attitude and performance information; also called scanning.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the two fundamental skills of attitude instrument flying; instrument interpretation is the second.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Instrument Cross-Check”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: continuous and logical observation of instruments for attitude
notes.example: Like a lifeguard sweeping the pool in a steady pattern rather than watching one swimmer.

notes.front: What is the radial scan (selected radial cross-check)?
notes.back: A cross-check that keeps the eyes mainly on the attitude indicator, with quick glances out to the other flight instruments and back.
notes.explanation: The eyes move out and back like spokes from a hub, and the manoeuvre decides which instruments are included.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Selected Radial Cross-Check”, PDF p. 144
notes.evidence: 80 to 90 percent of flight time looking at the attitude indicator,
notes.example: Like a chef who keeps her eyes on the main pan and glances at each side dish, always coming back to the pan between them.

notes.front: In the cross-check, what is fixation?
notes.back: Staring at a single instrument.
notes.explanation: The handbook says it usually happens for a reason but has poor results.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 144
notes.evidence: Fixation, or staring at a single instrument, usually occurs for a reason, but has poor results.
notes.example: Like a driver staring at the satnav so long that the car drifts across the lane.

notes.front: In the cross-check, what is omission?
notes.back: Leaving an instrument out of the cross-check.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it another likely fault, often from failing to anticipate what an instrument will show after an attitude change.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 146
notes.evidence: Omission of an instrument from a cross-check is another
notes.example: Like checking your mirrors and speed on a motorway but never the fuel gauge.

notes.front: In the cross-check, what is emphasis?
notes.back: Relying on one instrument instead of on the combination of instruments needed for attitude information.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it an understandable fault early in training, but reliance on a single instrument is poor technique.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 146
notes.evidence: Emphasis on a single instrument, instead of on the combination
notes.example: Like judging a patient only by temperature and ignoring pulse and breathing, because the thermometer is the easiest to read.

notes.front: In the control and performance method, which indicators are the control instruments?
notes.back: The attitude and power indicators.
notes.explanation: They show immediate attitude and power and are calibrated so adjustments can be made in precise amounts.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Control Instruments”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: by reference to the attitude and power indicators.

notes.front: Which instruments are the performance instruments, and what do they show?
notes.back: The altimeter, airspeed indicator and VSI; they show the aircraft’s actual performance.
notes.explanation: They tell the pilot whether the attitude and power chosen are producing the result wanted.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Performance Instruments”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: The performance instruments indicate the aircraft’s actual performance. Performance is determined by reference to

notes.front: What do the navigation instruments show, in the control and performance grouping?
notes.back: The aircraft’s position relative to a selected navigation facility or fix.
notes.explanation: The group includes course indicators, range indicators, glideslope indicators and bearing pointers.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Navigation Instruments”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: The navigation instruments indicate the position of the aircraft

notes.front: In the control and performance method, is the vertical speed indicator a control or a performance instrument?
notes.back: A performance instrument.
notes.explanation: It shows the result of the attitude and power set, not the setting itself.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Performance Instruments”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: the altimeter, airspeed, or vertical speed indicator (VSI).

notes.front: In the control and performance method, is the tachometer a control or a performance instrument?
notes.back: A control instrument: it is a power indicator.
notes.explanation: Power indicators vary by aircraft and may include manifold pressure, tachometers and fuel flow.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Control Instruments”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: pressure, tachometers, fuel flow, etc.

notes.front: Control and performance, step 1: what do you do first?
notes.back: Establish an attitude and power setting on the control instruments that gives the desired performance.
notes.explanation: Known or computed attitude changes and approximate power settings reduce the workload.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Procedural Steps in Using Control and Performance”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: 1. Establish an attitude and power setting on the

notes.front: Control and performance, step 2: what comes after setting attitude and power?
notes.back: Trim until control pressures are neutralised.
notes.explanation: Trimming for hands-off flight is essential for smooth, precise control and frees attention for other duties.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Procedural Steps in Using Control and Performance”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: 2. Trim (fine tune the control forces) until control pressures are neutralized.

notes.front: Control and performance, step 3: what do you check once trimmed?
notes.back: Cross-check the performance instruments to see whether the attitude and power are giving the desired performance.
notes.explanation: The cross-check means both seeing and interpreting; a deviation’s size and direction set the correction.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Procedural Steps in Using Control and Performance”, PDF p. 136
notes.evidence: 3. Cross-check the performance instruments to determine if the established attitude or power setting is providing

notes.front: Control and performance, step 4: what do you do if performance is off?
notes.back: Adjust the attitude and/or power setting on the control instruments as necessary.
notes.explanation: The loop then repeats: set, trim, cross-check, adjust.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Procedural Steps in Using Control and Performance”, PDF p. 136
notes.evidence: 4. Adjust the attitude and/or power setting on the control

notes.front: Level at 5,000 feet, you see the altimeter creeping up 50 feet with power unchanged. Using control and performance, what do you change?
notes.back: C: lower the pitch attitude slightly, re-trim, then cross-check.
notes.choices:
A) Re-trim alone until the climb stops
B) Chase the altimeter with elevator until it stops
C) Lower the pitch attitude slightly on the attitude indicator, then re-trim and cross-check
notes.choicesExplained: B: the method adjusts the control instruments, not the performance readout. A: the handbook says trim alone to change attitude usually gives erratic control.
notes.explanation: In this method the performance instruments show the error and the fix is made on the control instruments.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Procedural Steps in Using Control and Performance”, PDF p. 136
notes.evidence: 4. Adjust the attitude and/or power setting on the control

notes.front: What usually happens if trim alone is used to change the aircraft’s attitude?
notes.back: Erratic aircraft control.
notes.explanation: The handbook pairs control pressure first with trim afterwards for smooth, precise attitude changes.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Airplane Trim”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: Use of trim alone to establish a change in aircraft attitude usually results in erratic aircraft control.

notes.front: Control and performance versus primary and supporting: what is the same and what differs?
notes.back: Both use the same instruments and responses; they differ in reliance on the attitude indicator and how other instruments are interpreted.
notes.explanation: They are two ways of teaching the same flying, not two different sets of instruments.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Learning Methods”, PDF p. 135
notes.evidence: the attitude indicator and interpretation of other instruments.

notes.front: In straight-and-level flight, the {{c1::altimeter}} is normally the primary pitch instrument.
notes.explanation: It supplies the most pertinent altitude information when an exact altitude is to be held.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Pitch Control”, PDF p. 167
notes.evidence: this handbook, the altimeter is normally considered as the primary pitch instrument during level flight.

notes.front: In straight-and-level flight, which instrument is primary for bank?
notes.back: The heading indicator.
notes.explanation: Straight flight means zero bank at a constant heading, and the heading indicator supplies the most pertinent heading information.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Example of Primary and Support Instruments”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: or heading information and is primary for bank.

notes.front: In straight-and-level flight at constant airspeed, which instrument is primary for power?
notes.back: The airspeed indicator.
notes.explanation: In level flight it supplies the most pertinent information on performance in terms of power output.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Example of Primary and Support Instruments”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: in terms of power output and is primary for power.

notes.front: When is the attitude indicator the primary instrument, in the primary and supporting method?
notes.back: Only when trying to fly a specific bank angle or pitch angle; otherwise it acts as a control instrument.
notes.explanation: Primary instruments are those held at a constant reading, and the attitude indicator is held constant only when a precise angle is the target.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Attitude Indicator”, PDF p. 199
notes.evidence: the only time that the attitude indicator is a primary instrument is when attempting to fly at a specific

notes.front: In a stabilised constant-airspeed climb, which instrument is primary for pitch?
notes.back: The airspeed indicator.
notes.explanation: In a constant-airspeed climb the airspeed is the value held constant, so it becomes primary for pitch; the heading indicator stays primary for bank.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Climbs”, PDF p. 208
notes.evidence: attitude, the primary flight instrument for pitch will be the ASI

notes.front: In a standard-rate turn, which instrument is primary for bank?
notes.back: The turn rate indicator (turn coordinator).
notes.explanation: The aim is a standard rate of turn, so the instrument that shows rate of turn is the one held constant.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Turns”, PDF p. 212
notes.evidence: turn rate indicator since the goal is to achieve a standard rate

notes.front: Cruising level, you want to hold exactly 7,000 feet. Using primary and supporting, which instrument do you treat as primary for pitch?
notes.back: B: the altimeter.
notes.choices:
A) The attitude indicator
B) The altimeter
C) The vertical speed indicator
notes.choicesExplained: A: the attitude indicator is primary only when flying a specific pitch or bank angle. C: the VSI supports pitch but does not show the exact altitude being held.
notes.explanation: The handbook normally treats the altimeter as primary for pitch in level flight.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Pitch Control”, PDF p. 167
notes.evidence: this handbook, the altimeter is normally considered as the primary pitch instrument during level flight.

notes.front: On a long straight leg you must keep the wings level on a 090° heading. Which instrument is primary for bank?
notes.back: B: the heading indicator.
notes.choices:
A) The turn coordinator
B) The heading indicator
C) The magnetic compass
notes.choicesExplained: A: the turn coordinator is primary for bank in a standard-rate turn, not in straight flight. C: the compass is a backup, prone to errors in manoeuvres.
notes.explanation: In straight flight the heading is what must stay constant, and the heading indicator shows it most directly.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Example of Primary and Support Instruments”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: or heading information and is primary for bank.

notes.front: Level at 4,000 feet, you have slowed from 120 to 100 knots and are now holding 100 knots. Which instrument is primary for power?
notes.back: B: the airspeed indicator.
notes.choices:
A) The tachometer
B) The airspeed indicator
C) The altimeter
notes.choicesExplained: A: the tachometer is primary only for a moment while the power is being changed; once the new speed is held it is the supporting power instrument. C: the altimeter is primary for pitch in level flight.
notes.explanation: In level flight the airspeed indicator is primary for power, since holding airspeed is what power is for.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Example of Primary and Support Instruments”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: in terms of power output and is primary for power.

notes.front: Is cross-checking optional once the aircraft is trimmed in instrument flight?
notes.back: No: cross-checking is mandatory in instrument flying.
notes.explanation: Human error, instrument error and performance differences mean performance never stays constant for long.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Instrument Cross-Check”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: Cross-checking is mandatory in instrument flying.

notes.front: What are the two fundamental skills of attitude instrument flying?
notes.back: Instrument cross-check and instrument interpretation.
notes.explanation: They are learned separately but must be joined into smooth, positive control.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Fundamental Skills”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: and instrument interpretation, both resulting in positive

notes.front: During a descent to an assigned altitude, which instruments should get most of your cross-check?
notes.back: Those giving the most pertinent information for that phase, usually the ones to be held at a constant reading.
notes.explanation: The handbook recommends no single fixed pattern; the manoeuvre decides which instruments matter most.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Instrument Cross-Check”, PDF p. 143
notes.evidence: no specific method of cross-checking is recommended

notes.front: In the radial scan, do the eyes move directly from one outer flight instrument to another?
notes.back: No: they always return by way of the attitude indicator.
notes.explanation: The attitude indicator is the hub the other flight instruments are checked from.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Selected Radial Cross-Check”, PDF p. 144
notes.evidence: With this method, the pilot’s eyes never travel directly between the flight

notes.front: Rolling out of a turn, a student stares at the heading indicator waiting for 180° and finds the altimeter 150 feet low. Which cross-check error is this?
notes.back: A: fixation.
notes.choices:
A) Fixation
B) Omission
C) Emphasis
notes.choicesExplained: B: omission is leaving an instrument out of the scan altogether, not staring at one. C: emphasis is leaning on one instrument for attitude, such as holding altitude by the attitude indicator alone.
notes.explanation: Staring at one instrument lets the others drift unseen, which is what fixation means.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 144
notes.evidence: Fixation, or staring at a single instrument, usually occurs for a reason, but has poor results.

notes.front: What often causes omission of an instrument from the cross-check?
notes.back: Failing to anticipate significant instrument indications after an attitude change.
notes.explanation: If the pilot does not expect an instrument to change, it tends to drop out of the scan.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 146
notes.evidence: likely fault. It may be caused by failure to anticipate

notes.front: After levelling off, you watch the attitude indicator and altimeter carefully but have not looked at the heading indicator for two minutes. It now reads 20° off. Which error is this?
notes.back: C: omission.
notes.choices:
A) Fixation
B) Emphasis
C) Omission
notes.choicesExplained: A: you were not staring at one instrument. B: emphasis is relying on one instrument for attitude; here an instrument was simply left out.
notes.explanation: An instrument left out of the scan cannot warn of its drift, which is what omission produces.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 146
notes.evidence: Omission of an instrument from a cross-check is another

notes.front: Why does emphasis happen, according to the handbook?
notes.back: It is a natural tendency to rely on the instrument that is most readily understood, even when it gives wrong or inadequate information.
notes.explanation: The handbook still calls reliance on a single instrument poor technique.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 146
notes.evidence: readily understood, even when it provides erroneous or

notes.front: A pilot holds the miniature aircraft exactly on the horizon line and never looks at the altimeter, yet keeps wandering ±80 feet. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: B: include the altimeter in the cross-check.
notes.choices:
A) Watch the attitude indicator even more closely
B) Include the altimeter in the cross-check
C) Trim more often
notes.choicesExplained: A: that deepens the emphasis error. C: trim does not show altitude.
notes.explanation: The attitude indicator gives reasonably close altitude control, but not precise control without the altimeter.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 6 “Airplane Attitude Instrument Flying Using Analog Instrumentation”, “Common Cross-Check Errors”, PDF p. 146
notes.evidence: hold altitude with precision without including the altimeter

notes.front: A standard-rate turn is {{c1::3° per second}}.
notes.explanation: At that rate a full 360° takes two minutes, which is why two-minute turn instruments are marked for it.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 5 “Flight Instruments”, “Turn-and-Slip Indicator”, PDF p. 116
notes.evidence: doghouse. A standard rate turn is 3° per second.

notes.front: What is the handbook’s rule of thumb for the bank angle of a standard-rate turn?
notes.back: Divide the airspeed by 10 and add half the result.
notes.explanation: The bank needed for a standard rate varies with true airspeed, so a faster aircraft needs more bank.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Turns to Predetermined Headings”, PDF p. 181
notes.evidence: divide the airspeed by 10 and add one-half the result.

notes.front: Using the rule of thumb, about what bank angle gives a standard-rate turn at 140 knots?
notes.back: About 21°.
notes.explanation: 140 ÷ 10 = 14, plus half of 14 (7) gives 21°.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Turns to Predetermined Headings”, PDF p. 181
notes.evidence: divide the airspeed by 10 and add one-half the result.

notes.front: What are two conditions the handbook lists as causes of unusual attitudes?
notes.back: Two of: turbulence, disorientation, instrument failure, preoccupation with flight deck duties (among others).
notes.explanation: The list also includes confusion, careless cross-checking, errors in interpretation and lack of proficiency.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Unusual Attitudes and Recoveries”, PDF p. 187
notes.evidence: disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, preoccupation with flight deck duties, carelessness in cross-checking,

notes.front: Whenever you see an instrument rate of movement or indication unlike the basic instrument manoeuvres, what should you assume and do?
notes.back: Assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check to confirm the attitude, instrument error or malfunction.
notes.explanation: A faster cross-check confirms whether it is a real attitude, an instrument error or a malfunction.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Recognizing Unusual Attitudes”, PDF p. 188
notes.evidence: attitude and increase the speed of cross-check to confirm the

notes.front: When you notice an unusual attitude, what is the immediate problem?
notes.back: What the aircraft is doing and how to get it back to straight-and-level quickly, not how it got there.
notes.explanation: The aim is to return to straight-and-level flight as quickly as possible.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Recovery from Unusual Attitudes”, PDF p. 188
notes.evidence: the immediate problem is not how the airplane got there, but

notes.front: Altimeter unwinding fast, airspeed rising into the yellow arc, turn coordinator showing a left turn. Which unusual attitude is this?
notes.back: B: nose-low, diving left turn.
notes.choices:
A) Nose-high, climbing left turn
B) Nose-low, diving left turn
C) Level left turn
notes.choicesExplained: A: a nose-high attitude shows the altimeter rising and the airspeed falling. C: a level turn would hold altitude and airspeed.
notes.explanation: Nose-low attitudes show on the same instruments as nose-high ones, but with the needles moving the opposite way.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Recognizing Unusual Attitudes”, PDF p. 188

notes.front: Nose-high unusual attitude with airspeed decreasing: what are the recovery actions, in order?
notes.back: Increase power as needed, apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose, then level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder.
notes.explanation: Lowering the nose early prevents a stall; the actions are almost simultaneous but follow that sequence.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Nose-High Attitudes”, PDF p. 188
notes.evidence: nose and prevent a stall, and correct the bank by applying

notes.front: You look up from a chart to find airspeed falling through 70 knots, altimeter climbing and a right bank. What is your first control action after adding power?
notes.back: B: forward elevator pressure to lower the nose.
notes.choices:
A) Level the wings first
B) Forward elevator pressure to lower the nose
C) Reduce power
notes.choicesExplained: A: in a nose-high recovery the bank is corrected after the nose is lowered. C: reducing power is the nose-low recovery.
notes.explanation: With airspeed decaying, the handbook’s sequence is power, then nose down to prevent a stall, then bank.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Nose-High Attitudes”, PDF p. 188
notes.evidence: nose and prevent a stall, and correct the bank by applying

notes.front: Nose-low unusual attitude with airspeed increasing: what are the recovery actions, in order?
notes.back: Reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose to level flight with smooth back pressure.
notes.explanation: Reducing power prevents excessive airspeed and loss of altitude; the handbook then corrects bank before pitch.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Nose-Low Attitudes”, PDF p. 189
notes.evidence: Raise the nose to level flight attitude by applying smooth back elevator pressure.

notes.front: In a nose-low unusual attitude, what instinctive reaction must you resist?
notes.back: Pulling back on the elevator control first.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this a very important point: the correct order is power, then bank, then pitch.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Nose-Low Attitudes”, PDF p. 189

notes.front: In cloud you find a 45° left bank, nose down, airspeed rising fast. What do you do first?
notes.back: C: reduce power.
notes.choices:
A) Add full power
B) Pull back hard on the elevator
C) Reduce power
notes.choicesExplained: B: pulling back is the instinctive but wrong first reaction; the nose is raised only after the wings are level. A: power is added in the nose-high recovery, not here.
notes.explanation: The handbook starts a nose-low recovery by reducing power to prevent excessive airspeed and loss of altitude.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers”, “Nose-Low Attitudes”, PDF p. 189

notes.front: After inadvertent or unintended entry into instrument meteorological conditions, what does the Airman Certification Standards expect you to know?
notes.back: The procedures available to safely regain visual meteorological conditions.
notes.explanation: The standard lists this beside unusual-attitude recovery, prevention and the use of automation.
notes.source: Instrument Rating – Airplane ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8C), Area IV, Task B “Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Procedures available to safely regain visual meteorological conditions (VMC) after flight into inadvertent instrument meteorological conditions

notes.front: Which of these does the Airman Certification Standards list as a situation that could lead to loss of control in flight?
notes.back: A: task saturation.
notes.choices:
A) Task saturation
B) A current navigation database
C) A briefed alternate airport
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: these are good practice, not causes of loss of control.
notes.explanation: The standard names stress, task saturation, an inadequate scan with distractions, and spatial disorientation.
notes.source: Instrument Rating – Airplane ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8C), Area IV, Task B “Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Situations that could lead to loss of control in-flight (LOC-I) or unusual attitudes in-flight (e.g., stress, task saturation, inadequate instrument scan distractions, and spatial disorientation).

notes.front: What does the handbook say the autopilot should be used for?
notes.back: To reduce workload, giving the pilot more time to monitor the flight.
notes.explanation: It adds that autopilot use also lowers the chance of entering an unusual attitude.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Autopilot Usage”, PDF p. 219
notes.evidence: The autopilot should be utilized to reduce workload, which affords the pilot more time to monitor the flight.

notes.front: Single-pilot in cloud, you must copy a long reroute and reprogramme the navigator. What use of the autopilot does the handbook support?
notes.back: B: engage it to cut workload, and keep monitoring.
notes.choices:
A) Disconnect it so you stay in the loop
B) Engage it to cut workload and keep monitoring the flight
C) Engage it and stop cross-checking until you finish
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook recommends the autopilot to reduce workload. C: the time saved is meant for monitoring, not for dropping the cross-check.
notes.explanation: The autopilot frees time, and that time is for monitoring the flight.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 7 “Airplane Basic Flight Maneuvers Using an Electronic Flight Display”, “Autopilot Usage”, PDF p. 219
notes.evidence: The autopilot should be utilized to reduce workload, which affords the pilot more time to monitor the flight.

notes.front: Which sensory system is responsible for most of the illusions that lead to spatial disorientation?
notes.back: The vestibular system.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that visual illusions can also cause spatial disorientation.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Illusions Leading to Spatial Disorientation”, PDF p. 72
notes.evidence: leading to spatial disorientation is the vestibular system.

notes.front: How can “the leans” start, according to the handbook?
notes.back: A bank entered too slowly to be sensed, then corrected abruptly, gives the illusion of banking the other way.
notes.explanation: The slow entry does not move the fluid in the roll canals, but the abrupt correction does.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “The Leans”, PDF p. 72
notes.evidence: fluid in motion, creating the illusion of a banked attitude to

notes.front: After slowly drifting into a left bank in cloud, you snap the wings level and now feel banked right. What do you do?
notes.back: A: trust the attitude indicator and keep the wings level.
notes.choices:
A) Trust the attitude indicator, keep the wings level and cross-check
B) Roll left until the feeling of bank goes away
C) Look out for a horizon
notes.choicesExplained: B: rolling to match the feeling puts the aircraft back into the original bank. C: in cloud there is no reliable outside reference.
notes.explanation: The disoriented pilot may roll back into the original bank or lean until the illusion passes; the instruments show the truth.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “The Leans”, PDF p. 72
notes.evidence: the right. The disoriented pilot may make the error of rolling

notes.front: In a graveyard spiral, what does the pilot feel and do?
notes.back: Feels level while in a turn that is losing height, pulls back to stop the descent, and tightens the spiral.
notes.explanation: A prolonged coordinated turn feels like no turn, so the altitude loss is read as a level descent.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Graveyard Spiral”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: attempt to climb or stop the descent. This action tightens the

notes.front: After several minutes in a gentle turn in cloud, you feel level but the altimeter is unwinding. Your instinct is to pull back. What should you do instead?
notes.back: A: level the wings first by the attitude indicator.
notes.choices:
A) Level the wings by the attitude indicator, then correct pitch
B) Pull back to stop the descent
C) Add power and hold the turn
notes.choicesExplained: B: pulling back in a bank tightens the spiral and increases the loss of altitude. C: holding the turn keeps the spiral going.
notes.explanation: The handbook says pulling back without levelling tightens the spiral and increases the height loss.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Graveyard Spiral”, PDF p. 73

notes.front: What sets off the Coriolis illusion?
notes.back: Moving the head in a different plane after being in a turn long enough for the ear fluid to move with the canal.
notes.explanation: The head movement sets the fluid moving again and creates a sense of turning or accelerating on another axis.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Coriolis Illusion”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: speed as the canal. A movement of the head in a different

notes.front: Midway through a long standard-rate turn in cloud, you drop your pen. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: B: retrieve it with minimal head movement.
notes.choices:
A) Duck down quickly to grab it
B) Retrieve it with minimal head movement, alert for the Coriolis illusion
C) Leave it and look over your shoulder for traffic
notes.choicesExplained: A: a quick head movement in another plane is exactly what triggers the illusion. C: a large head turn during a prolonged turn has the same risk.
notes.explanation: This is why the handbook wants a cross-check with minimal head movement.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Coriolis Illusion”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: retrieve it with minimal head movement and be alert for

notes.front: What illusion can a rapid acceleration, as on take-off, produce, and what may the pilot do?
notes.back: A feeling of being nose-up (the somatogravic illusion); the pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude.
notes.explanation: Acceleration stimulates the otolith organs the same way as tilting the head back, especially without good visual references.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Somatogravic Illusion”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: good visual references. The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low or dive attitude.

notes.front: Taking off into a dark night over the sea with no lights ahead, you accelerate fast and feel the nose pitching steeply up. What should you do?
notes.back: C: hold the planned attitude on the instruments.
notes.choices:
A) Look outside for a horizon
B) Lower the nose until the feeling stops
C) Hold the planned climb attitude on the attitude indicator
notes.choicesExplained: B: pushing to cure the feeling can put the aircraft into a dive near the ground. A: there is no reliable visual horizon.
notes.explanation: The somatogravic illusion is strongest without good visual references, so the instruments must win.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Somatogravic Illusion”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: of being in a nose-up attitude, especially in situations without

notes.front: What can an abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight cause?
notes.back: The inversion illusion: a feeling of tumbling backwards.
notes.explanation: The pilot may push abruptly into a nose-low attitude, which can make the illusion stronger.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Inversion Illusion”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can stimulate the otolith organs enough to create the illusion of

notes.front: An updraft gives an abrupt upward acceleration. What illusion can follow, and what may the pilot do?
notes.back: The elevator illusion of climbing; the pilot may push into a nose-low attitude.
notes.explanation: A downdraft has the opposite effect, and the pilot may pull the nose up.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Elevator Illusion”, PDF p. 73
notes.evidence: illusion of being in a climb. This is called elevator illusion.

notes.front: What are two things that can create a false horizon?
notes.back: A sloping cloud formation; an obscured horizon (among others).
notes.explanation: The handbook’s list also includes an aurora, a dark scene of ground lights and stars, and geometric patterns of ground lights.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “False Horizon”, PDF p. 74
notes.evidence: A sloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, an aurora

notes.front: In the dark, what happens to a stationary light you stare at for many seconds?
notes.back: It appears to move (autokinesis).
notes.explanation: The pilot may lose control trying to line the aircraft up with the light’s false movements.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Autokinesis”, PDF p. 74
notes.evidence: In the dark, a stationary light will appear to move about when

notes.front: What does the handbook call the most important way to cope with spatial disorientation?
notes.back: Become proficient with the flight instruments, rely on them and disregard your sensory perceptions.
notes.explanation: The sensations cannot be fully prevented, but training and awareness let pilots ignore them.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Coping with Spatial Disorientation”, PDF p. 76
notes.evidence: instruments and disregard your sensory perceptions.

notes.front: When does the handbook say to avoid sudden head movements?
notes.back: Particularly during take-offs, turns and approaches to landing.
notes.explanation: Head movement is what sets off the Coriolis illusion described in the same chapter.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Coping with Spatial Disorientation”, PDF p. 75
notes.evidence: 6. Avoid sudden head movement, particularly during

notes.front: Unless proficient on instruments, into what should you not continue flight?
notes.back: Adverse weather, or dusk or darkness.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds keeping night currency and proficiency if flying at night.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Coping with Spatial Disorientation”, PDF p. 75
notes.evidence: 4. Do not continue flight into adverse weather conditions

notes.front: Flying on instruments in turbulence, you feel strongly that you are climbing in a right turn, but the instruments show level flight on heading. What do you do?
notes.back: A: believe the instruments.
notes.choices:
A) Believe the instruments and keep cross-checking
B) Correct toward what you feel
C) Split the difference
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook says judgements of attitude based on bodily sensations are frequently false. C: any correction toward the feeling moves the aircraft away from the correct attitude.
notes.explanation: Rely on the instruments and disregard sensory perceptions, as the handbook puts it.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 3 “Human Factors”, “Coping with Spatial Disorientation”, PDF p. 76
notes.evidence: instruments and disregard your sensory perceptions.

notes.front: What usually identifies an analogue system or instrument failure?
notes.back: A warning indicator, or an inconsistency between the attitude indicator and the supporting performance instruments.
notes.explanation: Keep control of the aircraft first, then speed up the cross-check to find the failed component.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 11 “Emergency Operations”, “Analog Instrument Failure”, PDF p. 332
notes.evidence: A warning indicator, or an inconsistency between indications

notes.front: One quick way to find a failed gyro: compare the attitude indicator with which two instruments?
notes.back: The rate-of-turn indicator and the vertical speed indicator.
notes.explanation: This compares instruments on different systems, so the odd one out shows which system failed.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 11 “Emergency Operations”, “Analog Instrument Failure”, PDF p. 332
notes.evidence: comparison of the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn

notes.front: In cloud the attitude indicator shows a steady 20° left bank, but the turn coordinator is level, the heading steady and the VSI at zero. What is most likely?
notes.back: A: the attitude indicator has failed.
notes.choices:
A) The attitude indicator has failed
B) The turn coordinator and VSI have both failed
C) The aircraft is in a 20° left bank
notes.choicesExplained: C: a real bank would show on the turn coordinator and heading. B: two instruments on separate systems agreeing makes the lone attitude indicator the likely fault.
notes.explanation: An inconsistency between the attitude indicator and the supporting instruments usually identifies the failure.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), ch. 11 “Emergency Operations”, “Analog Instrument Failure”, PDF p. 332
notes.evidence: comparison of the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn
